```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(reticulate)
```

Wikipedia pages where the data already lives in a clean HTML table. These scrape directly with `pandas.read_html()`, no text parsing required.

* [List of social networking services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_social_networking_services): name, type, focus/audience.
* [List of defunct social networking services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_defunct_social_networking_services): name, type, focus. Covers the platforms this generation grew up on and lost (Myspace, Vine, AIM).
* [List of recessions in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_recessions_in_the_United_States): name, period, duration, peak unemployment, GDP decline. Spans the dot-com bust and the 2008 financial crisis.
* [List of cryptocurrencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cryptocurrencies): year introduced, currency, founder, consensus mechanism.
* [List of countries by minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_minimum_wage): country, nominal and PPP (purchasing power parity) annual/hourly wage, percent of GDP per capita.
* [List of Disney Channel original films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Disney_Channel_Original_Movies): year, film, premiere date, US viewership in millions.
* [History of the web browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_web_browser): a "Historical web browsers" table with Browser, Years, and per-OS support columns.
* [List of search engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_search_engines): a "Defunct or acquired" table with Name, Backend ownership, and Demise columns. Covers the Ask Jeeves, AltaVista, and Lycos era.
* [Comparison of cross-platform instant messaging clients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_cross-platform_instant_messaging_clients): Developer, Initial release, Platform, Latest release, license, monthly active users.
* [iPod, "Models and features" table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPod#Models_and_features): Model, Generation, Capacity, Connection, Original release date, Minimum OS to sync, Rated battery life.
* [Comparison of online dating services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_online_dating_services): Name, Owner, Registered users, Free, All features free, Hetero/polyamorous connections, Free messaging, STD-notification.

## Scraping method

Two examples below. Both fetch the raw page with `requests`, then hand the HTML to `pandas.read_html()`, which finds every table on the page and returns each as a DataFrame. Passing `match=` picks out the one table we want by a string that appears in its header.

The "List of recessions in the United States" table has a flat header, so renaming the columns is enough.

```{python}
#| label: scrape-recessions
#| eval: false
import io
import pandas as pd
import requests

url = "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_recessions_in_the_United_States"
html = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "wikimill-project/0.1"}).text

tables = pd.read_html(io.StringIO(html), match="GDP decline")
recessions = tables[0]
recessions.columns = [
    "name", "period_range", "duration", "time_since_previous",
    "peak_unemployment", "gdp_decline", "characteristics"
]
recessions.to_csv("data/recessions.csv", index=False)
recessions.head()
```

The "List of countries by minimum wage" table has a nested header: the annual and hourly figures are each split into nominal and PPP sub-columns. `pandas` reads this as a `MultiIndex`, so we flatten it into single column names before saving.

```{python}
#| label: scrape-minimum-wage
#| eval: false
wage_html = requests.get(
    "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_minimum_wage",
    headers={"User-Agent": "wikimill-project/0.1"}
).text
tables = pd.read_html(io.StringIO(wage_html), match="Minimum wage")
wage = tables[0]
wage.columns = ["_".join(c for c in col if "Unnamed" not in c).strip("_")
                for col in wage.columns.to_flat_index()]
wage.to_csv("data/minimum_wage.csv", index=False)
wage.head()
```

The "Comparison of online dating services" table mixes a registered-user count with a reporting year in one free-text cell, and the "Free" and "All features free" columns hold full sentences rather than a plain Yes/No. We save the raw columns as-is here, the parsing happens in R below.

```{python}
#| label: scrape-dating
#| eval: false
dating_html = requests.get(
    "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_online_dating_services",
    headers={"User-Agent": "wikimill-project/0.1"}
).text
tables = pd.read_html(io.StringIO(dating_html), match="Registered users")
dating = tables[0]
dating.columns = [
    "name", "description", "owner", "registered_users", "free",
    "all_features_free", "hetero", "poly", "free_messaging", "std_notification"
]
dating.to_csv("data/dating_services.csv", index=False)
dating.head()
```

These chunks are shown for reference only (`eval: false`), rendering the site doesn't hit Wikipedia. Run `python src/scrape_recessions.py`, `python src/scrape_minimum_wage.py`, and `python src/scrape_dating.py` from the project root to refresh the raw CSVs in `data/`.

## Data manipulation in R

The recessions CSV stores its numbers as text. This extracts the start year and the percentages, labels the dot-com, financial crisis, and COVID-19 recessions by era, and keeps recessions since 1945 with a recorded GDP decline. It also tags each recession with the generation that was around 22, typical career-entry age, when it started, using the standard Pew Research birth-year brackets.

```{r}
#| label: clean-recessions
#| message: false
#| collapse: true
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)

generation_levels <- c(
  "Greatest Generation", "Silent Generation", "Baby Boomers",
  "Generation X", "Millennials", "Generation Z"
)

recessions <- read_csv("data/recessions.csv") |>
  mutate(
    start_year = as.integer(str_extract(period_range, "\\d{4}")),
    gdp_decline_pct = as.numeric(str_extract(gdp_decline, "[\\d.]+")),
    peak_unemployment_pct = as.numeric(str_extract(peak_unemployment, "[\\d.]+")),
    era = case_when(
      start_year %in% 2001 ~ "Dot-com bust",
      start_year %in% 2007:2009 ~ "Financial crisis",
      start_year %in% 2020 ~ "COVID-19",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    entry_birth_year = start_year - 22L,
    generation = case_when(
      entry_birth_year < 1928 ~ "Greatest Generation",
      entry_birth_year < 1946 ~ "Silent Generation",
      entry_birth_year < 1965 ~ "Baby Boomers",
      entry_birth_year < 1981 ~ "Generation X",
      entry_birth_year < 1997 ~ "Millennials",
      TRUE ~ "Generation Z"
    ),
    generation = factor(generation, levels = generation_levels)
  ) |>
  filter(start_year >= 1945, !is.na(gdp_decline_pct))
```

```{r}
#| label: view-recessions
#| collapse: true
write_csv(recessions, "data/recessions_clean.csv")
recessions
```

For the minimum wage data, this keeps the country and nominal annual wage columns and drops rows with no wage on record.

```{r}
#| label: clean-minimum-wage
#| collapse: true
wage_clean <- read_csv("data/minimum_wage.csv") |>
  select(matches("Country"), matches("Annual_Nominal")) |>
  rename(country = 1, annual_wage_usd = 2) |>
  mutate(annual_wage_usd = as.double(annual_wage_usd)) |>
  filter(!is.na(annual_wage_usd))
```

```{r}
#| label: view-minimum-wage
#| collapse: true
write_csv(wage_clean, "data/minimum_wage_clean.csv")
wage_clean
```

The registered-user count and the reporting year are both embedded in one string, like `"30,000,000 as of 2006[2]"`. The user count always has thousands separators, so matching a comma-grouped number pulls it out first; whatever's left over is where the year lives. The "Free" and "All features free" columns are full sentences, we keep the first word (Yes/No/Maybe) as a clean category and leave the original text in place.

```{r}
#| label: clean-dating
#| message: false
#| collapse: true
dating_clean <- read_csv("data/dating_services.csv") |>
  mutate(
    users_raw = str_extract(registered_users, "\\d{1,3}(?:,\\d{3})+"),
    registered_users_n = as.numeric(str_remove_all(users_raw, ",")),
    users_year = as.integer(str_extract(str_remove(registered_users, fixed(users_raw)), "\\d{4}")),
    free_clean = str_extract(free, regex("^(Yes|No|Maybe)", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    all_features_free_clean = str_extract(all_features_free, regex("^(Yes|No|Maybe)", ignore_case = TRUE))
  ) |>
  select(-users_raw) |>
  filter(!is.na(registered_users_n)) |>
  distinct(name, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: view-dating
#| collapse: true
write_csv(dating_clean, "data/dating_services_clean.csv")
dating_clean
```
